LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
The Lagos Neighborhood Safety Corps (LNSC) is a uniformed security agency established by a law of the Lagos State House of Assembly in 2016 to assist the Police and other security agencies to maintain law and order in the state.
Neighbourhood is also known a community is a place or area where person lives as a community.
Security is the state of being free from danger, threat or crime.

Neighbourhood security is a community security that helps to protect the entire community from crime.
Neighbourhood security is also called community security.

Neighbourhood security watch is a group of security who watches over the neighborhood’s properties as a way of preventing crime.

assist the Police and other security agencies -

INTRODUCTION TO NEIGHBOURHOOD SECURITY: MEANING OF NEIGHBOURHOOD, NEIGHBOURHOOD SECURITY AND THINGS UP A NEIGHBOURHOOD
SECURITY EDUCATION
PRIMARY 4 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 1
THEME -  PERSONAL AND NEIGHBOURHOOD SECURITY
PREVIOUS LESSON -
TOPIC - INTRODUCTION TO NEIGHBOURHOOD SECURITY
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning, Examples and Importance of Neighbourhood
3. Meaning of Neighbourhood Security and Things That Make Up a Neighbourhood
4. People Who Help to Keep the Neighbourhood Safe
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of a neighbourhood.
2. Explain the meaning of neighbourhood security.
3. Identify the things that make up a neighbourhood.
4. Mention people who help to keep the neighbourhood safe.
5. State ways of promoting neighbourhood security.
6. Explain the importance of neighbourhood security.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have learned about their home, family, and community. They also know some important places in their surroundings such as schools, markets, and places of worship.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing the concept of neighbourhood security and the need to keep the community safe.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Charts or pictures of a neighbourhood
2. Pictures of houses, schools, markets, hospitals, police stations, and places of worship
3. Pictures of police officers, security guards, and community leaders
4. Flashcards
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every one of us lives in a neighbourhood where we have houses, schools, markets, roads, places of worship, and other important facilities. We also see people such as police officers, security guards, community leaders, and parents who help to keep the neighbourhood safe. When everyone obeys the rules and reports suspicious activities, the neighbourhood becomes peaceful and secure.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of a neighbourhood, the meaning of neighbourhood security, the things that make up a neighbourhood, and how everyone can help to keep the neighbourhood safe.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF NEIGHBOURHOOD
A neighbourhood is the area or community where people live together. It includes the houses, roads, schools, markets, and other places around our homes.
MEANING OF NEIGHBOURHOOD SECURITY
Neighbourhood security means protecting the people and property in a neighbourhood to make it safe and peaceful for everyone.
Neighbourhood security involves everyone working together to prevent crime and report suspicious activities.
IMPORTANCE OF NEIGHBOURHOOD SECURITY
Neighbourhood security helps to:
1. Protect lives and property.
2. Prevent crime.
3. Promote peace and unity.
4. Make people feel safe.
5. Encourage community development.
6. Build good relationships among neighbours.
LESSON 2 - THINGS THAT MAKE UP A NEIGHBOURHOOD
A neighbourhood is made up of:
1. Houses - Places where people and families live.
2. Roads and Streets - Paths used by people and vehicles to move from one place to another.
3. Schools - Places where children and adults go to learn.
4. Markets - Places where people buy and sell goods.
5. Hospitals or Health Centres - Places where sick or injured people receive medical treatment.
6. Police Station - A place where police officers work to maintain law and order and protect the community.
7. Places of Worship (Churches and Mosques) - Places where people gather to pray and worship God.
8. Parks and Playgrounds - Open spaces where people relax, exercise, and children play.
9. Shops - Small business places where people buy everyday items such as food, clothing, and household goods.
10. People living in the Community - The men, women, and children who live in the neighbourhood and work together to make it a safe and peaceful place.
LESSON 3 - PEOPLE WHO HELP TO KEEP THE NEIGHBOURHOOD SAFE
1. Police Officers - They enforce the law, prevent crime, and protect people and property.
2. Neighbourhood Watch Members - They work with residents to observe and report suspicious activities in the community.
3. Security Guards - They protect homes, schools, offices, and other public places from danger.
4. Community Leaders - They guide community members, help settle disputes, and promote peace and order.
5. Parents - They teach children safety rules and help protect their families and neighbourhood.
6. Responsible Citizens - They obey the law, report crimes or suspicious activities, protect public property, and cooperate with security officers to keep the neighbourhood safe.
WAYS TO PROMOTE NEIGHBOURHOOD SECURITY
1. Obey community rules.
2. Report suspicious people or activities.
3. Avoid fighting and stealing.
4. Protect public property.
5. Keep the environment clean.
6. Know your neighbours.
7. Do not give information to strangers.
8. Cooperate with security officers.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. A neighbourhood is _______.
A. a building used as a market
B. a place where only teachers livemarket
C. the area where people live together
D. a place where only children play

C. locking the classroom door
B. protecting people and property in the community
C. buying and selling goods
D. travelling from one town to another

A. Police station
B. School
C. Market
D. Airport runway

A. Police officers
B. Traders
C. Farmers
D. Drivers

A. Ignoring community rules
B. Damaging public property
C. Fighting with neighbours
D. Reporting suspicious activities

Use the following words to complete the sentences: houses, community, security, police, market,
6. A neighbourhood is also called a _______.
7. People live in _______.
8. The _______ helps people to buy and sell goods.
9. _______ officers help to maintain law and order.
10. Neighbourhood _______ protects lives and property.
C. True or False
11. Schools are part of a neighbourhood. _______
12. Everyone has a role to play in keeping the neighbourhood safe. _______
13. Responsible citizens should report suspicious activities. _______
14. Hospitals are not found in a neighbourhood. _______
15. Community leaders help to promote peace and order. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. School - A. Keeps law and order
17. Market - B. Place for relaxation and play

20. Park - E. Place where goods are bought and sold

2. B. protecting people and property in the community

14. A. Police officers

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that a neighbourhood is the area or community where people live together. They also learned that neighbourhood security means protecting the people and property in the community to make it safe and peaceful for everyone.
Pupils identified the things that make up a neighbourhood, such as houses, roads, schools, markets, hospitals, police stations, places of worship, parks, and shops.
They also learned about the people who help to keep the neighbourhood safe, including police officers, neighbourhood watch members, security guards, community leaders, parents, and responsible citizens.
Finally, pupils understood that everyone has a role to play in promoting neighbourhood security by obeying rules, reporting suspicious activities, protecting public property, keeping the environment clean, and cooperating with security officers. These actions help to promote peace, safety, unity, and development in the neighbourhood.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction - The teacher displays a picture or chart of a neighbourhood showing houses, roads, schools, markets, a police station, and places of worship. The teacher asks pupils to identify the places they can see before introducing the topic Introduction to Neighbourhood Security.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the places in the picture and mention similar places in their own neighbourhood.
Step 2: Meaning of Neighbourhood - The teacher explains that a neighbourhood is the area or community where people live together. Also, the teacher gives examples of neighbourhoods around the school and pupils’ homes.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of a neighbourhood and mention the name of their own neighbourhood.
Step 3: Meaning of Neighbourhood Security - The teacher explains that neighbourhood security means protecting the people and property in the community to keep everyone safe. Also, the teacher discusses why security is important.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of neighbourhood security and give examples of safe behaviour.
Step 4: Things That Make Up a Neighbourhood - The teacher explains the important places found in a neighbourhood, such as:
- Houses
- Roads
- Schools
- Markets
- Hospitals
- Police stations
- Places of worship
- Parks
- Shops
The teacher uses charts and pictures for illustration.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify and describe the different places found in a neighbourhood.
Step 5: People Who Help to Keep the Neighbourhood Safe - The teacher introduces the people responsible for neighbourhood security, including:
- Police officers
- Neighbourhood watch members
- Security guards
- Community leaders
- Parents
- Responsible citizens
The teacher explains the role of each person.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify the duties of each person in maintaining neighbourhood security.
Step 6: Group Activity - The teacher divides the class into four groups and assigns the following tasks:
- Group 1: Explain the meaning of neighbourhood.
- Group 2: List the things that make up a neighbourhood.
- Group 3: Identify the people who help to keep the neighbourhood safe.
- Group 4: Discuss ways pupils can help to promote neighbourhood security.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, identify, and present their group work.
Step 7: Lesson Summary - The teacher reviews the meaning of neighbourhood, neighbourhood security, the things that make up a neighbourhood, and the people who help to keep the community safe.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation - The teacher asks oral and written questions and assesses pupils’ understanding of neighbourhood security.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the evaluation questions, identify important places in a neighbourhood, and explain how they can help to keep their neighbourhood safe.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Types of Neighbourhood: Meaning, Examples and Identifying Places in Your Neighbourhood | Primary 4 (Basic 4) First Term Week 2 Security Education
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils to,
1. Explain the meaning of a neighbourhood.
2. Explain the meaning of neighbourhood security.
3. Identify at least five things that make up a neighbourhood.
4. Mention at least five people who help to keep the neighbourhood safe.
5. State at least five ways of promoting neighbourhood security.
6. Explain the importance of neighbourhood security in protecting lives and property.

SECURITY EDUCATION
PRIMARY 4 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 3
THEME -  NEIGHBOURHOOD
PREVIOUS LESSON - Types of Neighbourhood: Meaning, Examples and Identifying Places in Your Neighbourhood | Primary 4 (Basic 4) First Term Week 2 Security Education
TOPIC - GOOD AND GOOD NEIGHBOURHOOD
LEARNING
1. Introduction
2. Meaning and Characteristics of Good Neighbourhood
3. Meaning and Characteristics of Bad Neighbourhood
4. Classification of Neighbourhood Types
5. How to make a Neighbourhood Better
6. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
7. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of a good neighbourhood.
2. Explain the meaning of a bad neighbourhood.
3. Identify at least five features of a good neighbourhood.
4. Identify at least five features of a bad neighbourhood.
5. Classify neighbourhoods according to location and living conditions.
6. Suggest ways of making a neighbourhood cleaner, safer, and better.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the meaning of neighbourhood, the types of neighbourhood, and how to identify important places in their neighbourhood.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by helping pupils understand the difference between good and bad neighbourhoods and how neighbourhoods can be classified according to their location and living conditions.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures of clean and safe neighbourhoods
2. Pictures showing dirty or unsafe neighbourhoods
3. Charts showing urban and rural neighbourhoods
4. Flashcards showing features of good and bad neighbourhoods
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Many pupils have seen neighbourhoods that are clean, peaceful, and safe, while some places may have dirty surroundings, poor roads, insecurity, or disorder. The way people care for their environment and treat one another can affect the quality and safety of a neighbourhood.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of good and bad neighbourhoods, the features of each, how neighbourhoods can be classified according to their location and living conditions, and ways of making a neighbourhood clean, peaceful, and safe.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF A GOOD NEIGHBOURHOOD
A good neighbourhood is a place where people live peacefully and safely, keep their surroundings clean, and care about one another.
Features of a Good Neighbourhood
1. Clean and well-maintained surroundings
2. Safe roads and streets
3. Good houses and buildings
4. People respect one another
5. Neighbours help one another
6. Security personnel help protect people
7. Schools, health centres, and other useful facilities are available
8. People obey rules and laws
MEANING OF A BAD NEIGHBOURHOOD
A bad neighbourhood is a place where people may experience poor living conditions, insecurity, disorder, or lack of care for the environment.
Features of a Bad Neighbourhood
1. Dirty surroundings
2. Poorly maintained roads
3. Frequent crime or insecurity
4. Broken or poorly maintained buildings
5. Lack of important facilities
6. People do not respect one another
7. Poor waste disposal
8. Frequent fighting and disorder
LESSON 2 - CLASSIFICATION OF NEIGHBOURHOOD TYPES
Neighbourhoods can be classified in different ways.
1. Based on Location
- Urban neighbourhood: Found in towns and cities. It usually has many people, buildings, roads, businesses, schools, and other facilities.
- Rural neighbourhood: Found mainly in villages and the countryside. It usually has fewer people, fewer buildings, and more farmland and open spaces.
2. Based on Living Conditions
- Good neighbourhood: Has clean surroundings, safety, peace, useful facilities, and responsible residents.
- Bad neighbourhood: Has poor sanitation, insecurity, disorder, or inadequate facilities.
HOW TO MAKE A NEIGHBOURHOOD BETTER
Residents can improve their neighbourhood by:
1. Keeping the environment clean.
2. Disposing of waste properly.
3. Protecting public property.
4. Reporting suspicious activities to the appropriate authorities.
5. Respecting neighbours.
6. Obeying community rules.
7. Helping people in need.
8. Taking part in community sanitation and development activities.

6. A clean, peaceful, and safe neighbourhood is called a _______ neighbourhood.
7. A neighbourhood affected by insecurity, disorder, or poor sanitation may be described as a _______ neighbourhood.
8. A neighbourhood found in a town or city is usually an _______ neighbourhood.
9. A neighbourhood found mainly in a village or countryside is a _______ neighbourhood.

12. Dumping refuse everywhere helps to improve a neighbourhood. _______

15. Residents can help improve their neighbourhood by obeying community rules. _______
D. Match Column A with Column B.
Column A - Column B
16. Good neighbourhood - A. Usually found in villages and the countryside
17. Bad neighbourhood - B. Keeping the environment clean
18. Urban neighbourhood - C. A peaceful, safe, and clean place
19. Rural neighbourhood - D. A place affected by disorder or insecurity

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that a good neighbourhood is a clean, peaceful, safe, and well-organised place where people respect and help one another. A bad neighbourhood may have poor sanitation, insecurity, crime, fighting, and disorder.
Pupils also learned that neighbourhoods can be classified by location into urban and rural neighbourhoods. An urban neighbourhood is usually found in a city or town, while a rural neighbourhood is mainly found in a village or countryside.
They also learned that everyone can help to improve the neighbourhood by keeping the environment clean, obeying rules, respecting others, protecting public property, reporting unsafe activities, and taking part in community sanitation.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher shows pupils pictures of a clean, peaceful neighbourhood and a dirty, unsafe neighbourhood. The teacher asks pupils to identify what they notice in each picture.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and mention what makes each neighbourhood good or bad.
Step 2: Good Neighbourhood
The teacher explains that a good neighbourhood is a clean, peaceful, safe, and well-organised place where people respect and help one another.
The teacher discusses its features:
- Clean surroundings
- Peaceful environment
- Safe roads and streets
- Helpful neighbours
- Respect for others
- Proper waste disposal
- Obedience to community rules
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention things they can do to make their neighbourhood good.
Step 3: Bad Neighbourhood
The teacher explains that a bad neighbourhood is a place where there may be insecurity, poor sanitation, disorder, or lack of care for the environment.
Examples include:
- Dirty surroundings
- Poor waste disposal
- Frequent fighting
- Crime and insecurity
- Damaged public property
- Poorly maintained roads
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify behaviours that can make a neighbourhood bad.
Step 4: Classification of Neighbourhoods
The teacher explains that neighbourhoods can be classified according to their location and living conditions.
According to location:
- Urban neighbourhood: Usually found in towns and cities.
- Rural neighbourhood: Usually found in villages and the countryside.
According to living conditions:
- Good neighbourhood: Clean, peaceful, and safe.
- Bad neighbourhood: Dirty, unsafe, or disorderly.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils classify examples as urban, rural, good, or bad neighbourhoods.
Step 5: Making the Neighbourhood Better
The teacher explains ways pupils can help improve their neighbourhood:
- Keep the environment clean.
- Dispose of waste properly.
- Respect neighbours.
- Obey community rules.
- Protect public property.
- Report suspicious activities to responsible adults or security authorities.
- Take part in community sanitation.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils suggest other ways of keeping their neighbourhood clean and safe.
Step 6: Group Activity
The teacher divides the class into four groups:
- Group 1: List five features of a good neighbourhood.
- Group 2: List five features of a bad neighbourhood.
- Group 3: Explain the difference between urban and rural neighbourhoods.
- Group 4: Suggest five ways to improve a neighbourhood.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers.
Step 7: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning of good and bad neighbourhoods and the classification of neighbourhood types.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the main points of the lesson.
Step 8: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils the practice exercise to assess their understanding.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils complete the multiple choice, fill-in-the-gaps, true or false, and matching sections.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON

Teacher asks pupils to,
1. Explain the meaning of a good neighbourhood.
2. Explain the meaning of a bad neighbourhood.
3. Mention at least four features of a good neighbourhood.
4. Mention at least four features of a bad neighbourhood.
5. Differentiate between an urban neighbourhood and a rural neighbourhood.
6. Classify neighbourhoods according to location and living conditions.
7. Mention at least four ways of making a neighbourhood clean, peaceful, and safe.

This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how to identify strangers, understand the dangers they may pose, and practise personal safety measures.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION

In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of strangers, examples of strangers, the dangers they may pose, and the personal security measures they should follow to stay safe.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF A STRANGER (WHO IS A STRANGER?)
A stranger is a person you do not know or someone your parents or guardians have not introduced to you.
Examples of Strangers
Examples of strangers include:
1. A person you have never met before.
2. Someone who asks you to follow them.
3. A person who offers you gifts or sweets.
4. Someone who asks for your personal information.
5. A visitor you do not know.
DANGERS OF STRANGERS
Strangers can sometimes:
1. Trick children with gifts or money.
2. Ask children to follow them.
3. Kidnap children.
4. Steal from people.
5. Harm or deceive children.
Note: Not every stranger is a bad person, but children should always be careful and follow safety rules.
LESSON 2 - PERSONAL SECURITY MEASURES
To stay safe around strangers, pupils should:
1. Never follow a stranger.
2. Do not collect gifts, sweets, or money from strangers.
3. Do not share personal information with strangers.
4. Stay close to trusted adults.
5. Inform your parents, teachers, or guardians if a stranger approaches you.
6. Walk with friends or adults whenever possible.
7. Shout for help if you feel unsafe.
8. Know your home address and your parents’ phone numbers.
9. Avoid lonely places.
10. Report suspicious people to trusted adults or security officers.
IMPORTANCE OF PERSONAL SECURITY
Personal security helps pupils to:
1. Stay safe.
2. Avoid danger.
3. Protect themselves from strangers.
4. Build confidence.
5.Live peacefully in the community.

1. A stranger is ______.
A. someone you do not know
B. your brother
C. your teacher
D. your friend

SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that a stranger is someone they do not know or someone their parents or guardians have not introduced to them.
They identified examples of strangers, discussed the possible dangers of strangers, and learned that they should always be careful when dealing with people they do not know.
Pupils also learned important personal security measures, such as not following strangers, refusing gifts from strangers, avoiding sharing personal information, staying close to trusted adults, shouting for help when in danger, and reporting suspicious strangers to parents, teachers, or other trusted adults.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher displays pictures of children meeting strangers, a trusted adult helping a child, and a child refusing gifts from a stranger.
The teacher asks:
- Who is a stranger?
- Have you ever seen someone you did not know?
- What should you do if a stranger talks to you?
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and answer the questions.
Step 2: Meaning of a Stranger
The teacher explains that a stranger is someone you do not know or someone your parents or guardians have not introduced to you.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of a stranger in their own words.
Step 3: Examples of Strangers
The teacher explains examples of strangers:
- A person you have never met before.
- Someone who asks you to follow them.
- Someone who offers you gifts or sweets.
- A visitor you do not know.
- Someone asking for your personal information.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention other examples of strangers.
Step 4: Dangers of Strangers
The teacher explains that strangers may:
- Trick children with gifts.
- Ask children to follow them.
- Kidnap children.
- Steal from people.
- Harm or deceive children.
The teacher reminds pupils that not every stranger is bad, but they should always be careful.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the dangers of talking to strangers.
Step 5: Personal Security Measures
The teacher explains how pupils can stay safe by:
- Never following strangers.
- Refusing gifts from strangers.
- Not sharing personal information.
- Staying close to trusted adults.
- Reporting strangers to parents or teachers.
- Shouting for help when in danger.
- Avoiding lonely places.
- Walking with friends or trusted adults.

- Group 2: List five dangers of strangers.

Each group presents its work to the class.

The teacher reviews the meaning of strangers, examples, dangers, and personal security measures.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Pupils sometimes see people behaving strangely in their neighbourhood, such as someone hiding around houses, trying to enter a building secretly, or asking children to follow them. They may also notice abandoned bags or objects in public places. Such movements and activities may be signs of danger and should never be ignored.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the meaning of suspicious movement, identify suspicious activities in the neighbourhood, and learn the correct ways to respond to keep themselves and others safe.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT
Suspicious movement is any unusual or strange behaviour or movement that may threaten the safety of people or property.
MEANING OF SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITIES
Suspicious activities are actions that seem unusual, unsafe, or likely to cause harm.
Examples of Suspicious Activities in the Neighbourhood
1. A stranger hiding around houses.
2. Someone trying to break into a building.
3. A person carrying dangerous weapons.
4. Someone stealing or damaging property.
5. People fighting or causing violence.
6. A person asking children to follow them.
7. Someone moving around secretly at odd hours.
8. A suspicious bag or object left in a public place.
LESSON 2 - WHAT TO DO WHEN YOU NOTICE SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITIES
1. Stay calm.
2. Do not go close to the suspicious person or object.
3. Inform your parents, teacher, or another trusted adult.
4. Report the incident to the police or other security officers.
5. Move to a safe place if you are in danger.
6. Do not touch any suspicious object.
7. Encourage others to stay away from the danger.
IMPORTANCE OF REPORTING SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITIES
Reporting suspicious activities helps to:
1. Protect lives and property.
2. Prevent crime.
3. Keep the neighbourhood safe.
4. Help security officers do their work.
5. Promote peace in the community.

B. playing football

B. A teacher teaching in class
C. Children playing football

B. Report to a trusted adult

D. Ignore the situation

A. report it and stay away
B. open it

B. Trader’s association
C. Police officers

11. You should touch a suspicious object. ______
12. Suspicious activities should be reported. ______
13. The police help to protect lives and property. ______
14. You should follow a suspicious stranger. ______
15. Staying alert helps to keep people safe. ______

17. Police - B. Tell a trusted adult

9. police
10. safe

12. True
13. True
14. False
15. True

17. A - Protects lives and property

20. E - Staying away from danger
SUMMARY
In this lesson, pupils learned that suspicious movement is any unusual behaviour or movement that may threaten the safety of people or property.
They also learned that suspicious activities include actions such as hiding around buildings, attempting to break into houses, carrying dangerous weapons, leaving suspicious objects in public places, or trying to lure children away.
Pupils learned that they should stay calm, avoid suspicious people or objects, report suspicious activities to trusted adults or security officers, and move to a safe place if necessary. They also understood that reporting suspicious activities helps to keep the neighbourhood safe.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher displays pictures showing a suspicious person hiding near a building, a suspicious bag left in a public place, and a child reporting an incident to a police officer or trusted adult.
The teacher asks:
- What do you see in these pictures?
- Which actions look unusual or dangerous?
- What should you do if you notice something suspicious?
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils observe the pictures and answer the questions.
Step 2: Meaning of Suspicious Movement
The teacher explains that suspicious movement is unusual behaviour or movement that may threaten the safety of people or property.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of suspicious movement in their own words.
Step 3: Meaning and Examples of Suspicious Activities
The teacher explains that suspicious activities are actions that seem unsafe or likely to cause harm.
Examples include:
- Hiding around houses.
- Trying to break into a building.
- Carrying dangerous weapons.
- Stealing or damaging property.
- Asking children to follow strangers.
- Leaving suspicious objects in public places.
- Moving around secretly at odd hours.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify suspicious activities from pictures and examples.
Step 4: What to Do When You Notice Suspicious Activities
The teacher explains the safety steps:
- Stay calm.
- Do not go near the suspicious person or object.
- Inform a trusted adult.
- Report to the police or security officers.
- Move to a safe place if necessary.
- Do not touch suspicious objects.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss the correct actions to take.
Step 5: Importance of Reporting Suspicious Activities
The teacher explains that reporting suspicious activities helps to:
- Protect lives and property.
- Prevent crime.
- Keep the neighbourhood safe.
- Help security officers do their work.
- Promote peace in the community.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain why suspicious activities should be reported.

The teacher divides the class into four groups.

- Group 2: List five suspicious activities that may happen in the neighbourhood.

- Group 4: Role-play how to report suspicious activities to a trusted adult or security officer.
Each group presents its work to the class.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, role-play, and present their answers.

THEME -  GOVERNANCE

3. Differentiate between an urban neighbourhood and a rural neighbourhood.

5. Identify at least five places found in their neighbourhood.
6. Explain the importance of knowing places in their neighbourhood.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about the meaning of neighbourhood, neighbourhood security, and the things that make up a neighbourhood.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by introducing the types of neighbourhood and helping pupils identify important places in their own neighbourhood.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Every child lives in a neighbourhood. Some neighbourhoods are in busy towns and cities, while others are in quiet villages. Each neighbourhood has important places such as schools, markets, hospitals, roads, and places of worship that help people in their daily lives.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the types of neighbourhood, examples of urban and rural neighbourhoods, and how to identify important places in their own neighbourhood.
MEANING OF NEIGHBOURHOOD
A neighbourhood is the area or community where people live, work, learn, and interact with one another.
TYPES OF NEIGHBOURHOOD
1. Urban Neighbourhood
An urban neighbourhood is a neighbourhood located in a town or city. It has many people, many buildings, and good roads.
Examples:
- Ikeja
- Surulere
- Victoria Island
- Kano City
- Port Harcourt
Features of an Urban Neighbourhood
- Many houses and buildings
- Good road network
- Markets and shopping centres
- Schools and hospitals
- Banks and offices
- Heavy traffic
- Large population
2. Rural Neighbourhood
A rural neighbourhood is a neighbourhood found in villages or the countryside. It has fewer people and fewer buildings.
Examples:
- Farming villages
- Small rural communities
- Features of a Rural Neighbourhood
- Few houses
- Small population
- Farms and farmlands
- Fewer roads
- Fewer schools and hospitals
- Quiet environment
PLACES FOUND IN A NEIGHBOURHOOD
Common places found in a neighbourhood include:
- Houses
- Schools
- Markets
- Hospitals or health centres
- Police stations
- Fire service stations
- Churches and mosques
- Roads and streets
- Parks and playgrounds
- Shops
IMPORTANCE OF KNOWING PLACES IN YOUR NEIGHBOURHOOD
Knowing places in your neighbourhood helps you to:
1. Find your way easily.
2. Know where to get help during emergencies.
3. Stay safe.
4. Locate important public services.
5. Develop a sense of belonging.

Finally, they understood that knowing the places in their neighbourhood helps them find their way easily, stay safe, know where to get help during emergencies, and develop a sense of belonging to their community.

Rural Neighbourhood

SECURITY EDUCATION

1. Explain the meaning of reporting suspicious movement.
2. Identify the people to whom suspicious movements should be reported.
3. Explain the 5 Ws used when reporting suspicious movement.
4. State at least five ways to raise alarm during an emergency.
5. Demonstrate how to report suspicious movement correctly.
6. Explain the importance of reporting suspicious movement promptly.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about suspicious movement, types of suspicious movement, and how to identify suspicious activities.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils who to report suspicious movements to, how to raise alarm, and how to give useful information using the 5 Ws.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Pictures showing suspicious movements
2. Pictures of police officers, teachers, parents, and community security officers
3. Flashcards showing the 5 Ws

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Sometimes pupils may notice suspicious people or unusual activities in their homes, schools, or neighbourhoods. Knowing that something is suspicious is not enough; pupils must also know who to tell and how to give correct information. Reporting suspicious movement quickly and correctly helps adults and security officers respond in time to prevent danger.
In this lesson, pupils will learn who to report suspicious movement to, how to raise alarm safely, and how to use the 5 Ws to give clear and useful information when making a report.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF REPORTING SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT
Reporting suspicious movement means informing a trusted person or security officer about unusual or dangerous activities that may threaten lives or property.
PEOPLE TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT TO
Pupils should report suspicious movements to:
1. Parents or guardians - if you are at home.
2. Teachers - if you are at school.
3. The head teacher - if you are at school and need additional help.
4. Police officers - if you are on the road or in your community.
5. Community security officers or neighbourhood watch members - if you are at public events such as a naming ceremony, wedding, birthday party, festival, or community gathering.
6. Responsible community leaders - if your parents or guardians are not at home or are unavailable.
LESSON 2 - WAYS TO RAISE ALARM
When you notice suspicious movement, you can:
1. Inform a trusted adult immediately.
2. Shout loudly for help if they are in danger.
3. Call or ask an adult to call the police.
4. Tell a teacher or school authority.
5. Move quickly to a safe place.
6. Warn other people nearby without putting themselves in danger.
7. Stay calm while waiting for help.
HOW TO REPORT SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT
If you notice any suspicious movement, report it immediately to your parents, teachers, the police, or another trusted adult. When making a report, give clear information about what you saw.
Use the 5 Ws to make your report:
1. Who did you see?

2. When did you see it?
- For example: Around 12 noon.
3. Where did it happen?
- For example: At the school gate.
4. What was the person doing?
- For example: The person was peeping through the school gate.
5. Why did you think it was suspicious?
- For example: The person was examining the school gate padlock and looking around secretly.

“I saw a man around 12 noon at the school gate. He was peeping through the gate and examining the padlock. I think his behaviour was suspicious because he was looking around secretly.”

4. Give correct information when making a report.

- Who was involved?
- When did it happen?
- Where did it happen?
- What was the person doing?

They also learned different ways to raise alarm, such as shouting for help, informing trusted adults, and contacting security officers.

CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Pupils may sometimes notice people behaving strangely in their neighbourhood, such as hiding around buildings, following others secretly, trying to enter houses without permission, or leaving bags in public places. These actions may be signs of danger and should be taken seriously.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the different types of suspicious movement, how to identify suspicious activities, and the correct ways to stay safe and report such situations to trusted adults or security officers.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT
Suspicious movement is any unusual behaviour or movement that may threaten the safety of people or property.
TYPES OF SUSPICIOUS MOVEMENT
1. Loitering Around Buildings - A person staying around houses, schools, or offices without a clear reason.
2. Moving Around at Odd Hours - A person walking around suspiciously very late at night or very early in the morning.
3. Trying to Hide - A person hiding behind buildings, vehicles, or bushes.
4. Following People Secretly - A person secretly following another person without permission.
5. Trying to Enter a Building Without Permission - A person attempting to break into a house, school, or shop.
6. Carrying Dangerous Weapons - A person carrying weapons in a way that may threaten others.
7. Leaving Suspicious Objects - Someone leaving a bag, box, or package in a public place and walking away.
8. Watching People or Buildings Unusually - A person observing homes, schools, banks, or markets for a long time without a reason.
LESSON 2 - HOW TO IDENTIFY SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITIES
Pupils should watch for:
1. Unusual behaviour.
2. Strange movements.
3. Attempts to steal or damage property.
4. Unknown people asking children to follow them.
5. Suspicious objects left in public places.
6. People behaving in a secretive manner.
How to Stay Safe
1. Stay away from suspicious people or objects.
2. Do not touch suspicious bags or packages.
3. Inform your parents, teachers, or another trusted adult.
4. Report suspicious activities to the police or security officers.
5. Avoid lonely places.
6. Walk with trusted adults or friends.
7. Shout for help if you feel unsafe.
8. Stay calm during emergencies.
LESSON 3 - IMPORTANCE OF STAYING SAFE
Following safety rules helps pupils to:
1. Protect themselves from danger.
2. Prevent crime.
3. Protect lives and property.
4. Assist security officers.
5. Keep the neighbourhood peaceful.

They also learned how to identify suspicious activities and the importance of staying away from danger, reporting suspicious movements to trusted adults or security officers, and following personal safety rules to protect themselves and others.

INTRODUCTION

However, failing to report suspicious activities can lead to crime, injuries, or damage to property. Every pupil should know the importance of reporting suspicious activities to the right authorities so that help can come quickly and lives and property can be protected.
In this lesson, pupils will learn the consequences of not reporting suspicious activities or movements, the right authorities to report to, and why reporting suspicious activities promptly is important.
LESSON 1 - MEANING OF REPORTING SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITIES
Reporting suspicious activities means telling the right people about unusual or dangerous activities so that they can take action quickly.
CONSEQUENCES OF NOT REPORTING SUSPICIOUS ACTIVITIES OR MOVEMENTS
If suspicious activities are not reported:
1. Criminals may escape.
2. People may be injured.
3, Lives may be lost.
4. Property may be stolen or destroyed.
5. Crime may increase in the neighbourhood.
6. Children and other people may not be safe.
7. Peace in the community may be disturbed.
8. Security officers may not know about the danger in time.
LESSON 2 - THE RIGHT AUTHORITIES TO REPORT TO

3. Keep the neighbourhood peaceful.
4. Help security officers respond quickly.
5. Ensure everyone stays safe.
